draftNote: Draft — the hieroglyphs are read from the printed type of Budge's 1895 edition of the papyrus, and the signs and readings are still being checked; expect changes.
source: Papyrus of Ani (British Museum EA 10470), Plates XXIX, XXX. Hieroglyphs transcribed from the interlinear text of E. A. W. Budge, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum (London, 1895), pp. 189–193; Budge's transliteration and word-by-word English were used to check the reading of the signs and the sense, never for wording. Only the papyrus's own text is given: the passages Budge supplies from other papyri in his appendixes and footnotes are left out. Transliteration in the Leiden convention, with the reed written i; translation made fresh from the Egyptian. Shown left to right; the papyrus is written in columns read from the top down. The line under each word ("say") is the conventional Egyptological classroom pronunciation — a neutral e between consonants; ꜣ and ꜥ as a; w as u or w; ṯ as tj; ḏ as dj; ḫ and ẖ as kh; š as sh — an artificial teaching pronunciation, since the vowels of Egyptian were never written. The grouping of signs within a word follows Budge's type, which regularises the scribe's hand.
about: The introduction to Spell 125: Ani arrives at the Hall of the Two Truths, where the dead are judged, greets Osiris, and claims his purity by listing the holy places he has been to and the secret things he has seen; then Anubis, keeper of the door, questions him, and he must name the door and its two leaves before he may pass. Budge prints lines 1–18 under Plate 30 and then goes back to Plate 29 for lines 19–28; on the papyrus the spell goes on to the 42 declarations (Plates 31–32). Several passages are obscure or garbled in Ani's copy, and the notes say where.

sentences.i: Spell for entering the Hall of the Two Truths. Adoring Osiris, Foremost of the West.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes the title in red — rꜣ n ꜥq r, and dwꜣ — while the names of the hall and of the god stand in black. rꜣ is the mouth (r) with its stroke, 'utterance, spell'; n is the genitive 'of'. ꜥq 'enter' is the cormorant (ꜥq) with q as complement and the walking legs as classifier of motion; r 'into'. wsḫt 'broad hall' is spelled w-s-ḫ-t, with the hall sign as classifier and its t written again after it. mꜣꜥti 'the Two Truths' is the sickle (mꜣ) before the plinth (mꜣꜥ), t and the two strokes (-ti, the dual), and its classifiers double everything: two feathers of Maat, two cobra-goddesses, two town signs — Truth as a pair of goddesses and as a place. dwꜣ 'adore' is hand d and lasso wꜣ with a man raising his arms. wsir 'Osiris' is the seat (ws) and the eye (ir); ḫnty 'foremost' the three jars ḫnt with n, t and the y-strokes; imntt 'the West' the emblem of the West with t, t and the hill-country sign. This heading covers all of Spell 125: in this hall the heart is weighed, and the first thing the dead man does there is praise Osiris, king of the dead.

sentences.i: Words spoken by the Osiris, the scribe Ani, true of voice:
sentences.n: ḏd in, in red, is the standing formula that brings in a speech: ḏd 'say' (cobra ḏ + hand d; the print sets the hand under the curve of the cobra) and in 'by', the particle that names the speaker (reed i + water n). Wsir Ani, 'the Osiris Ani': the dead man carries the god's name, as one who will rise from death as Osiris did. sš 'scribe' is the scribe's palette, water-pot and pen alone. ꜣny 'Ani' is vulture ꜣ, water n and two reeds (y), with the seated man as classifier; the three small strokes under ꜣ-n belong to the usual writing of his name and are not read. mꜣꜥ-ḫrw (plinth mꜣꜥ + oar ḫrw) is 'true of voice': one whose words have been found true at the judgement, that is, vindicated. It follows Ani's name nearly every time.

sentences.i: I have come here to see your beauty.
sentences.n: ii·n·i 'I have come' is the sḏm·n·f, the past/perfect form: the verb ii 'come' (the reed-leaf ii with a reed i as complement and the walking legs), then the n that marks the form, then the seated man ·i 'I'. The next group is doubtful in the print: a long column-shaped sign over the road sign. It is read here as ꜥꜣ 'here, hither' (the column ꜥꜣ) with the road as classifier of direction; Budge takes it as a verb of motion. r + infinitive gives purpose: r mꜣꜣ 'to see' (sickle mꜣ, the eye as classifier, and vultures for ꜣ). nfrw 'beauty' is the heart-and-windpipe sign nfr written three times — the plural, used for an abstract — and ·k (the basket) is 'your': Ani speaks to Osiris.

sentences.i: My arms are (raised) in praise of your true name.
sentences.n: A sentence with no verb: the subject ꜥwy·i 'my two arms' and the adverbial phrase m iꜣw 'in praise' as its predicate. ꜥwy is the arm (ꜥ) written twice for the dual, with the dual strokes (y) and w; ·i 'my'. iꜣw 'praise, adoration' is reed i, vulture ꜣ, quail chick w, with the man raising his arms in worship as classifier. rn·k 'your name' (mouth r, water n, basket ·k). mꜣꜥ 'true' (sickle and plinth again) comes after the noun and its suffix, as Egyptian adjectives do. 'Raised' is not written: raised arms were simply the posture of praise. To know and praise a god's true name gave a claim on him.

sentences.l: have-come · I · here · not · came-into-being · cedar · not · (yet)-born · acacia · not · created · ground · tamarisk
sentences.i: I have come here, (where) the cedar has not come into being, the acacia has not (yet) been born, and the ground has not brought forth the tamarisk.
sentences.n: Three negative clauses follow ii·n·i ꜥꜣ. n ḫpr ꜥš: the negative n (two arms spread, D35), ḫpr 'come into being' (the scarab ḫpr, with r as complement), and ꜥš 'cedar' (arm ꜥ, pool š and a wood classifier whose printed form is uncertain; Budge adds a query). n ms·t šndt: msi 'give birth, be born' (the three fox-skins ms, s as complement, a woman giving birth as classifier) carries a t: this is the n sḏmt·f form, 'has not yet …'. šndt 'acacia' is the looped cord šn, d, t and a tree. The third n is Budge's restoration of damage. qmꜣw 'create, produce' (q, sickle mꜣ, vulture ꜣ, then a w — not needed if the ground is the subject, but it may be the w of the passive sḏm·w, 'the ground (and) the tamarisk have not been created' — and a bird on a perch that the print does not render cleanly), sꜣtw 'ground, soil' (pintail duck sꜣ, t, land sign, w), isr 'tamarisk' (i, s, r, tree, plural). What the clauses describe is uncertain: a place where no tree grows, or, with 'not yet', a time before the first trees. Ani's copy is obscure here.

sentences.l: when · entered · I · into · the-place · of-secret-things · words · my · (were) · with · Seth
sentences.i: When I entered the place of secret things, my words were with Seth.
sentences.n: ir + sḏm·f at the head of a sentence is 'when, if': ir ꜥq·i 'when I entered'. st 'place, seat' is the seat sign (st) with t and the house as classifier. The papyrus writes š-t-nw; read štꜣw. štꜣw 'secret things' is pool š, loaf t, and, where ꜣ is needed, a small pot that Budge's type gives the shape of the nw-pot (W24) — it stands for ꜣ in this word every time in the spell — then the crossed sticks and the papyrus roll as classifiers of the abstract, and the plural strokes. The papyrus writes a plain rod (coded U28, an approximation of the print) where the cobra ḏ is expected; read ḏdt·i. After it come d, t, the man with his hand to his mouth (speech), plural strokes and ·i. iw + a verb with this t would be an irregular sḏmt·f; read instead as the noun ḏdt 'words, speech' (ḏd + feminine t, plural strokes), it gives the ordinary sentence iw + subject + adverbial phrase: iw ḏdt·i ḥnꜥ stẖ 'my words were with Seth', that is, I spoke with him (Budge: 'I have spoken'). ḥnꜥ 'with' (wick ḥ, water n, arm ꜥ). Seth's name is written s-t with a small rectangle, a staff and the seated god: only s and t are read for certain (the rectangle, coded Q3 from the print, may be the pool š of the spelling stš), and the name is taken as stẖ, Seth (Budge: Sut), the god who killed Osiris.

sentences.i: My companion(?) drew near to me, his face covered, fallen upon the secret things.
sentences.n: ḫnm is the jug ḫnm with ḫ, n and m as complements and the nose as classifier — the verb 'smell, be joined with'. With ·i it is taken here as a noun, 'my companion', which is doubtful (Budge queries it too). tkn 'come near' (t, k, n, walking legs) comes after its subject, so it is probably the stative (noun + stative: 'my companion (was) come near'), and tkn m is 'come near to': im·i is m 'in, at' with ·i, for m becomes im before a suffix. ḥbs 'clothe, cover' (ḥ, b, s and a fringed cloth) stands before ḥr·f 'his face' (the face with its stroke and ·f): 'covered (was) his face'. ḫrw 'fallen' is ḫr 'fall' (ḫ, r) with the w of the stative and a falling man as classifier. ḫt štꜣw 'secret things': ḫt 'thing' is placenta ḫ, t and the papyrus roll; the papyrus writes š-t-nw again; read štꜣw. Whose face is covered — Seth's or the companion's — the text does not say; the whole passage is obscure.

sentences.i: The council of the gateways are spirits.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes ḏꜣ-nw-t-ḏꜣ-s; read ḏꜣḏꜣt. ḏꜣḏꜣt 'council, tribunal' is the fire-drill ḏꜣ twice, with the small pot again standing for ꜣ, and t, the plural strokes and the seated god as classifiers; the bolt s after the second ḏꜣ has no place in the word. nt is the feminine form of the genitive 'of' (n + t), agreeing with ḏꜣḏꜣt. sbḫyt 'gateways' (s, b, ḫ, two reeds, t, plural strokes) are the portals of the world below. iw + noun + m-phrase says what the subject is: m ꜣḫw 'as spirits' — the ꜣḫ, written with the crested ibis, is the glorified, effective dead. sentences.i: Anubis said to those on either side of him: 'The voice of a man who comes from Egypt!'
sentences.n: ḏd in brings in a new speaker (not in red this time). inpw 'Anubis' is reed i, water n, stool p, quail chick w and the seated god. gs 'side' (the half-loaf sign) with its stroke, then ·f, then the two strokes y: the dual ending is written after the suffix, gs·fy 'his two sides', and n gs·fy is 'to (those at) his two sides'. ḫrw 'voice' is the oar with w and the man with hand to mouth; s 'man' is the bolt with stroke and seated man (the genitive is direct: 'voice of a man'). iw 'coming' is a participle written with the walking legs, w, and the legs again. tꜣ-mri 'Egypt' is the land sign tꜣ, the hoe mr with r and i, a staff that the print does not render cleanly, and two town signs. Anubis, guardian of the cemetery, is the doorkeeper here, and he speaks about the newcomer to the gods beside him.

sentences.n: The papyrus writes b-n-t-w; read bnw, the Bennu, with the heron as classifier. di·f (the giving arm di, + ·f) followed by a second sḏm·f, pr·i 'that I go out', is the causative 'he caused me to come forth, he let me come forth'; pri 'go out' is the house sign pr with r and the walking legs. r ḏd·t·i: r with the sḏmt·f form means 'until …', 'until I spoke'. What the clause means here is not clear. Budge takes it as purpose, which would ease the sense, but purpose is r + infinitive, and the t followed by the suffix ·i points to the sḏmt·f, so the translation keeps 'until'. The papyrus writes the plain rod again (U28, an approximation of the print) where the cobra ḏ is expected; read ḏd·t·i. The Bennu, the sun's heron of Heliopolis, is the very image of coming forth into the day.

sentences.n: iw·k rḫ·tw 'you know': iw with ·k, and the stative of rḫ with the 2nd singular ending ·tw (t, w). The ir in front (reed, stroke, mouth) is taken as bringing in the question, as Budge takes it; it could also be 'if'. sbꜣ 'door' is the gateway sign alone. Budge reads it sebeχ, as if sbḫt 'portal'; but pn 'this' (stool p, water n) is masculine and agrees with sbꜣ 'door'. r ḏd 'so as to say' is r + infinitive. The lizard with plural strokes (ꜥšꜣ 'many') makes no clear sense here and is left out of the translation, as Budge leaves it. Knowing names is the theme of all that follows: the dead may pass a door only if he can name it.

sentences.n: Ani answers without a ḏd in. nb mꜣꜥt 'Lord of Maat' (basket nb; plinth mꜣꜥ, t, papyrus roll and plural strokes). ḥry tp, 'who is upon', is the nisba ḥry with tp 'head, top' (the head and stroke); rd·fy is the two legs with ·f and the dual y, 'his two feet'. in (reed, water) before rn is unexpected: it may be the particle in that marks the predicate ('it is …'), or a slip; it is rendered 'is'. stmt has a t this time.

sentences.l: lord · of-strength · marshaller · of-the-herds
sentences.i: 'Lord of strength, who marshals the herds' (is the name of the lower one).
sentences.n: The papyrus does not repeat 'is the name of the lower leaf': it is understood, and Budge supplies it in brackets. pḥty 'strength' is the hind-quarters pḥ, t, y and two lion's foreparts; ṯsw (the knotted cloth ṯs, s, w, and the low sign printed U15 for the forearm with stick) is from ṯs 'tie, raise up, marshal', 'one who marshals'. mnmnt 'cattle, herds' is the gaming-board mn with n, written twice, t, a bull and plural strokes. The numeral of line 25 stands inside mnmnt in Budge's print.

sentences.l: pass · yourself · you · know · Osiris · scribe · accounting · of-the-god's-offerings · of · gods · all · of-Thebes · Ani · true-of-voice · possessor · of-honour
sentences.i: Pass, then, for you know (it), Osiris, accounting scribe of the god's offerings of all the gods of Thebes, Ani, true of voice, possessor of honour.
sentences.n: Anubis lets him through. sš (bolt s, pool š, crossed sticks, walking legs) is taken as the imperative 'pass, go through'; the verb is not certain. ir·k is the preposition r with ·k, written with a reed before it, used after an imperative for emphasis ('pass, you!'). twk 'you' (t, w, k) is a later form of the independent pronoun, the subject of the stative rḫ·tw 'you know'. wsir again puts the eye first. sš ḥsb 'accounting scribe': ḥsb 'reckon' is a single round sign with the papyrus roll: the papyrus writes a round sign (coded Aa2 from the print, not a known writing of ḥsb); read ḥsb, from the sense and Budge's ḥesb. ḥtp-nṯr 'the god's offerings' joins two of Budge's groups as one word: the offering table ḥtp with t and p, and the god's flag with the seated god. nṯrw nbw 'all the gods' (nb with plural strokes is 'every, all'); wꜣst 'Thebes' is the wꜣs-sceptre with t and the town sign. nb imꜣḫ 'possessor of honour': imꜣḫ (the backbone sign with its stroke) is the honoured state of the blessed dead. Ani's copy of the dialogue ends here; other papyri (Budge's Appendix, from Naville's Todtenbuch) seem to carry it further, with the door-posts, the bolts and the floor of the hall each being named in turn before the dead may pass.
